A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MixAT research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original adversarial-training experiments, robustness and utility measurements, ablations, timing measurements and randomness analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds attack evaluations, training variants and sensitivity analyses in Appendix B.10–B.13.

M1.justification: The core MixAT objective, perturbation construction and batch mixing remain unchanged. Appendix B.10–B.11 adds limited procedural variants: precomputed GCG samples replace dynamically generated GCG samples in MixAT+GCG, and static GCG seeds replace PAP seeds in another ablation.

E1.justification: Appendix B.13 adds QueryAttack code/query-language attacks on Qwen2.5-14B and ArtPrompt ASCII-art attacks on Llama3-8B. These extend evaluation to substantially different input representations beyond the retained paraphrasing, suffix and other jailbreak scenarios. Existing training datasets and utility-task coverage remain.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain their defense baselines, including R2D2, CAT, LAT, RPO, PAT, PAP-AT and DUALAT where previously evaluated. QueryAttack and ArtPrompt reuse existing undefended, CAT and LAT comparators. The additional MixAT configurations are component ablations.

E3.justification: New ablations introduce precomputed-versus-dynamic GCG controls and half/double PGD perturbation budgets and step counts, with corresponding step-size adjustments (B.10–B.12). Main evaluation settings remain documented as before. Newly disclosed data filtering and sampling details do not establish changes to the existing experiments.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether precomputed GCG retains dynamic GCG's benefits, whether GCG can replace PAP seeds, and how continuous-attack hyperparameters affect robustness (Tables 17–19). These substantially strengthen examination of attack diversity and training design. Appendix C.2 also reports a qualitative comparison with a training-code bug fixed. Earlier ablations and the malicious-request case study are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.1 newly discloses fixed-seed sampling of the benign training subset, without specifying the seed value. The three-run training and attack evaluations and their uncertainty-reporting practices in B.2 remain unchanged. Revised MT-Bench means and standard deviations are result changes, not evidence of additional runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for two attack scenarios and three ablation studies in Tables 15–19. It also revises MT-Bench scores throughout existing tables and the LoRA utility plot: Table 1's Zephyr MixAT score changes from 54.3 to 52.2 and LAT-SFT from 54.4 to 32.6. The PDFs do not explain these revisions; main ASR entries remain unchanged. Section 4.1 additionally introduces an uncontextualized 18.75% score.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11, including the adversarial objective and MixAT/DUALAT perturbation sets, retain the same mathematical content. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs that are added or revised in v2.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: combining discrete and continuous adversarial training improves robustness–utility tradeoffs with modest computational overhead and generalizes across attacks. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly excludes model-tampering attacks and interprets the new GCG-seed results as evidence that attack diversity supports generalization. It also discusses PGD sensitivity and reusable static-GCG preparation costs. The discussion moved from Appendix D adds warnings about drawing broad robustness conclusions from individual attack types; its existing limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C substantially improves reproducibility documentation: the 256-token filtering threshold, 100 harmful queries with 1,188 continuations, 8,476 benign samples, and 7:1 interleaving procedure are newly specified. It discloses unintended gradient accumulation in the code underlying reported CAT/MixAT results and double quantization for Harmless evaluation. B.10 also supplies static-GCG generation times. These disclosures do not establish retraining of the main results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning model tampering, Constitutional AI and Constitutional Classifiers, positioning tampering outside scope and classifier defenses as complementary. QueryAttack and ArtPrompt are also newly cited for their evaluations. The broader positioning relative to discrete, continuous and latent adversarial training remains.

P1.justification: Appendix D's discussion moves into main-text Section 6 and is expanded, with the conclusion becoming Section 7. There are localized abstract and background edits, additional appendix subsections, and updated affiliation, acknowledgment and publication-header text. Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation expands with dedicated tables for new attack modalities, static-GCG comparisons and PGD sensitivity (Tables 15–19). Table 1 gains red/green cell shading, Figure 1a's adversarial-region boundary is redrawn, and Figure 4's utility curves change. Figure 6 is relocated with an expanded caption; the original example table is retained as Table 20.

improvement.justification: The new attack scenarios and component/sensitivity analyses strengthen evidence for generalization and clarify the importance of PAP-based training. Appendix C also makes important implementation choices and a training-code bug transparent. These gains improve an already extensive evaluation, but unexplained MT-Bench revisions and the new 18.75% statement with a higher-is-better scale inconsistent with ASR tables limit the net improvement.
